Area.evidence_source: This category is concerned with the processes and activities with which the young men engaged on their journey toward recovery from suicidality (see Figure 3). Participants repeatedly talked about their endeavors to find new meaning after their suicide attempt(s). These efforts were bound up with a sense of starting anew, deliberately restructuring their lives. There was a distinct process of leaving "what has gone" in the past, to some extent reframing how some of this past was viewed, and seeking a new perspective on their present and future. Identifying new meaning appeared, in some cases, to be prefaced with a growing sense of discontent and dissatisfaction with their lives: It just seemed like a lifetime of failure, like no sort of, you know, jumping from job to job. . . . I also, ehm, have a son from another relationship that I've never seen as well. It just seems, looking back on my adult life, it just stemmed from like one failure to another. And then the gambling on top of that, and it just, it just sort of seemed that everything, that my life was a complete failure. New meaning was variously conceived and pursued depending on a young man's individual circumstances and outlook. These included forming new, or renewing former, significant relationships; (re)developing family bonds; career and employment progression; personal development (e.g., voluntary work, acquiring new skills, returning to education); exploring spirituality-related issues; and helping others experiencing similar problems with suicide: So I took a positive approach to everything. I chose to do that, and that was the thing for me, like empowering. I chose to stop allowing it to happen to me. . . . And for me now, I have . . . worked with our own GPs [general practitioners] to promote mental health awareness, and to have different numbers for different groups.7 Frequently, finding (new) meaning in life was the direct opposite of the events and experiences that contributed to participants' increased suicidality in the first place. For example, although dysfunctional family dynamics was reported to be a significant contributor to suicidal ideation, having loving and supportive relationships with family members was described as bringing new meaning to their lives: "Now things have got very, very good. I have lovely children, and I have three boys, and I really enjoy my life now and I realize what I do have." The young men were also acutely aware of the powerful protective role that having close, concerned family members could play in relation to their risk of suicide. The (re)establishment of family bonds facilitated the development of a profound sense of guilt concerning the detrimental impact of their suicidal behavior on others and a consequent unwillingness to hurt their family (through the action of harming themselves): "But it's a dreadfully selfish thing, and I just . . . I couldn't deal with, handle the thought of how much pain I was going to be causing, well, my family and my friends." Finally, this category captures the importance of a developing appreciation among young men that recovery from their suicidality was, inevitably, a long-term process and that within this extended time frame, a degree of hard work was required: It took a while for us to make headway . . . but I guess I stuck with it and he [counselor] stuck with it, so we did make progress eventually, you know. At the start it didn't seem as if we were getting anywhere. This appreciation is integrally bound up with participants beginning to pick up the threads of their life and, in essence, learning to live again. For some, this process included making sense of their suicidality. None referred to this sense making in the past tense or as something they had completed. This shifted the sense of existential crisis from "What do I have to live for?" to "How do I go on living in the context of surviving a suicide attempt?" In addition, it was evident that a number of inter- and intrapersonal processes were involved, not least the continued support from MHPs and fellow travelers on the path to recovery: Every now and again the thought would still sorta creep in, but I've basically just, my plan has been trying to teach myself as not to have it as an option . . . So that's more or less worked, but like as I say, it just now and again sorta creeps in but I just keep . . . sorta tell myself that that can't be a choice, that's not an option. The regularity with which participants spoke of the need to make sense of their suicidality in the context of moving forward with their lives highlights the importance of these processes, particularly as they helped strengthen their connections with humanity.
